slides.text: As a master locksmith, I usually get called to estates after the funeral. The grieving widow, Mrs. Vance, led me down to the wine cellar of her late husband’s Victorian mansion and pointed to a six-foot walk-in Mosler bank vault. 'Arthur died of a stroke in his study three days ago,' she said, dabbing her eyes with a lace handkerchief. 'He never told me the combination.'

It took me four hours with a stethoscope and a tungsten drill rig to manipulate the four-wheel tumblers. When the heavy steel bolts finally retracted and I swung the twelve-inch door open, the smell of stale air hit me first. The vault was completely empty—except for ten broken fingernails embedded in the steel seam of the interior doorplate.

Scratched into the gunmetal paint on the inside of the door, carved with a wedding ring in the pitch dark, were the words: 'THAT IS NOT MY TWIN BROTHER UPSTAIRS. SHE LET HIM TAKE MY PLACE.' Behind me, at the top of the cellar stairs, Mrs. Vance quietly clicked the deadbolt shut and asked, 'Did you find anything, Mr. Miller?'
